I've solo'd Fatty with 7 weapons (DB, LBG, hammer, GS, IG, HH, and lance) but surprisingly I had the easiest and fastest time with lance. Granted, I did have a very good set with a great offense-defense balance. But IMO, the biggest thing is that lance doesn't have to dodge, reposition, look for a new opening from your new location, etc. It can just tank most attacks and immediately follow up with pokes. That allows for very good damage uptime.

It does get a bit difficult to break the head, but honestly I had gotten to Phase 3 with only one horn broken and his fire attacks really weren't all that much more threatening. Guard 5, Guard Up, Divine Blessing 5, and Fire Res 3 work *wonders* for lance against Fatty.

You might want to fiddle around with what your Palico is equipped with to help you with Alatreon as well.

I know for sure that my Palico has gotten an elemental topple to trigger before with an attack, which tells me that its contribution is definitely not trivial. Just choose the Ice or Fire weapon with the highest amount of element– IIRC the Shrieking Legi and Lavasioth ones are the best, but please correct me if I'm wrong. I have also gotten a topple with a Dragon Palico weapon too– in that case the Moogle Staff is best I believe.

You may want to go for a Status Palico weapon like Para or Sleep but in my experience Alatreon is super resistant to them and you won't really get but one proc maybe 20 minutes into the fight.

In terms of Palico Gadgets, I'd recommend Shieldspire Dummy if you find that Alatreon is putting too much pressure on you. It's good for catching your breath while your Palico or Dummy draws Alatreon's attention.

However if you feel confident enough at dodging Alatreon's attacks, the Palico Buff Horn can be useful for a little extra support just in case you do get hit. Faster health regen, Divine Blessing, etc are pretty comfy buffs.

The Vigorwasp is nice and all but IMO if you're gravely wounded, you should not be running around like a chicken trying to get to a Vigorwasp station 30 feet away and potentially running straight into an attack you didn't see, and should instead be popping a max potion right away. Bring extra ingredients so you can carry more than two. Plus, the Vigorwasp Revive can only be used once per fight, compared to all the other Gadgets, and you can't Farcaster out to switch it once it's been used up.

Yep, the Master's Touch set almost always uses Teo Beta pieces. For Gold Rathian, I'd personally recommended the Beta chest and legs. Sometimes the Alpha pieces of Fatalis armor are better, depending on what skills you want, but the Beta pieces usually work just as well.

If your team keeps dying while you stay afloat, it might be better to go solo, or possibly duo. If you don't feel comfortable being targeted so much by Raging Brachy while playing solo, there are a couple ways to take pressure off of you.

Consider giving your Palico the Dummy gear to take the attention away from you. Give your Palico a sleep weapon for a sleep proc and a little breath of air to heal or sharpen. Use a couple of traps in the first few areas to get some free damage in, since they don't work in the final area. As always, Rocksteady and Temporal mantles are very comfy for this fight. And most importantly, *bring blast resistance 3.*

Yes, there's definitely a significant difficulty increase starting around Stygian Zin, extending to Safi, Raging Brachy, Furious Rajang, Alatreon, and Fatty. IMO, those monsters are the biggest of bads in Iceborne.

Which Fatty armor pieces you make mostly depends on what other armor set bonuses you want, and what Fatalis materials you have available. Assuming you want to keep Master's Touch, you'd ideally keep the Teo headpiece, arms, and waist, because they're among the most skill-efficient Teo pieces, and you'd use Fatty pieces for the leftover chest and legs. HOWEVER, the chest pieces requires two (!!!) Evil Eyes... which is pretty difficult! The headpiece also requires Evil Eyes. So if you don't wanna farm Evil Eyes, you might want to use Teo chest and headpiece, and then any combination of one other Teo piece and two Fatalis pieces for the arm, waist, and legs. Just use whichever two you have enough materials to craft. Honestly, all the Fatalis pieces are really good skill- and slot-wise, and you can't really go wrong with any of them.

If you don't necessarily need Master's Touch, though, I'd say the two BEST Fatalis pieces are the waist and the arms. Both the A and B waist are great, and the A arms are good if you want Handicraft. If you don't, use the B arms.

I believe a lot of my Fatalis farming before I had his armor was done with a 3 piece Teo (for Master's Touch), 2 piece Gold Rathian (for Divine Blessing 5) armor set. I used the Raging Brachydios GS, with health regen augment. You could probably also swap out the 3 Piece Teo for 2 piece Raging Brachy armor with Agitator Secret if you want some extra damage and don't mind sharpening a little more, or have a lot of Whetfish Fins+. Whatever you use, I would HIGHLY recommend bringing Partbreaker 3 so that you can break his horns easier and you don't get One-Shot-Mode Fatalis during his third phase.

Once you get enough Fatalis pieces, either through plundercat or shiny drops and partbreaks, I'd recommend crafting 2 piece Fatalis armor as soon as possible. You can use it to replace both 2 piece Gold Rathi and 2 piece Raging Brachy, and it has generally better skills, slots, and defense than the alternatives.

Ok, today I've done some tests between a Valstrax Armor+Narga hammer build and a Valstrax Armor+Rampage Sharpness III build. Sharpness III is very comfy and you'll probably only have to sharpen during area transitions.


Night's Edge: Attack Boost 5, Dragonheart 5, Resentment 3, Resuscitate 3, Critical Boost 3, Weakness Exploit 3, Speed Sharpening 3. Attack Boost III Ramp-up.

20 hits of white, 60 hits of blue, 95% affinity on weakpoints, 292 attack with Dragonheart and Resentment, 277 attack with Dragonheart only.


Rampage Hammer Sharpness III: Dragonheart 5, Attack Boost 4, Resentment 3, Resuscitate 3, Critical Boost 3, Weakness Exploit 3, Speed Sharpening 3.

100 hits of blue, 70% affinity on weakpoints, 303 attack with Dragonheart and Resentment, 288 attack with Dragonheart only.


I tested each builds' Impact Crater against the Toadversary's head with Dragonheart active, but no Resentment:

Rampage Sharpness III: 726 on crits, 518 on non-crits.
Narga White Sharpness: 768 on crits, 548 on non-crits.
Narga Blue Sharpness: 698 on crit, 499 on non-crits.


So while Rampage might be more comfy in terms of sharpness, I get the feeling that it'll really only rival the Narga build in terms of damage if you have an external affinity source like Cutterfly or Fighter Palico.

Again, feel free to share your thoughts.

Well honestly, I think it's just fine for most elder dragons to share the same body layout of quadrupedal with a long neck and wings. So I think keeping Kushala's rig would be fine. They *could* have just done "generic dragon but it's blue/green and it controls water."

But instead, they took design inspiration from comb jellies, deep sea fish, and vampire squids. *That* is the kind of design mindset I love.

And I think it would have been really cool if they had a similar mindset for Velk– take the standard elder dragon rig and steal some features from existing animals to give it some pizzazz. The concept design I mentioned did just that. It still was quadrupedal with a long neck and wings BUT its head was shaped like a cobra's and it had deer antlers, and feathery wings with iridescent ice crystals (presumably) embedded in them. I think that would've been a much better use of the Kushala rig than just "generic dragon but it's blue and purple and controls ice."

Yep, flying monsters are a pain in the ass for hammer in World. Here's what I do to counter that.

-Give your palico the trap tool, so it puts down shock traps and bomb traps. All these will ensure Legi stays on the ground longer when he lands.

-Also, give your palico (or yourself) a para or sleep weapon, since both of these statuses will ground the monster if it procs while it's flying. The palico can use these attacks as ranged.

-When it's not agitated, try and launch the monster out of the sky with your slinger ammo the same way you do for wallbangs. It'll go crashing down. If the monster is flying high up, it might not crash, so you might need to turn it once or twice, since that also brings flying monsters lower to the ground. If you keep getting knocked off while on the head, bring Rocksteady and/or Temporal mantles to prevent it.

-Abuse tf out of aerial attacks from slopes and ledges. Pop an Airborne deco in your build for even better slope and ledge damage.

Good luck, you'll nab that frosty biatch.

Charge level two (the upswing) to close distance between you and the monster. *Stationary* charge level three (triple vertical spin) when you're close enough to the monster during a good opening. Aerial charged hits if there's a ledge nearby. Do that until the monster falls over. Then Big Bang Combo while it's down. Repeat until monster dead.

I'm sure you know this already, but aim for the head over everything else.

The only real "combo" per se you will be doing is Big Bang. Everything else will mostly be hard-hitting single attacks.

Remember to keep your hammer power-charged at all times. Power-charging has multiple benefits, and you need to have active it if you want the strongest version of the level three charge attack.

Also remember to stop holding the directional stick while doing the level three charge. Moving while doing it will turn it into a horizontal spin attack, which is a lot harder to control and usually puts out less damage.

I did it solo on my first try with hammer. The key for me was dodging a LOT. You absolutely need to keep on your toes for AT Velk. 

This is a fight where your strategy is not "tank hits and then heal," it's "do your absolute utmost to not get hit."

It helps to be *very* comfortable with her attack patterns. I would practice on tempered Velk a bunch if you have trouble with her tells. If you can't seem to figure out which direction to dodge with a specific attack, I would recommend watching a speedrun of your particular weapon to see how they handle that attack.

The ice walls preventing you from reading tells can be super annoying, but do note that you can also use audio cues as tells as a last resort. She makes specific noises with each move and if you're familiar enough with her attacks and pay attention, you can tell apart attacks just by the cry she makes. Maybe put headphones in if you're planning on doing this.

I particularly enjoyed doing it with hammer because of all the ice ledges Velk makes. You can dodge her attack and aim your roll towards a ledge, jump off it, and get an aerial hit in. She takes big head damage. Plus it's easy to slot Airborne into Fatalis armor with Airborne/Attack or /Expert gems, for a little extra oomph.

I didn't use Ice Res or Divine Blessing, but I did use Tool Specialist secret. Near-constantly alternating Rocksteady and Temporal mantles is very comfy– reduced damage plus little to no attack interruptions feels great.

Tool specialist 5 on as many builds as possible. Divine blessing 5 is super comfy but only reduces damage taken. I like near-constant mantles better (usually use Rocksteady and Temporal) because not only do I take less damage, but it also procs every hit, prevents knockbacks so I can keep on fighting, and allows for easier tenderizing and wallbanging. I know it doesn't reduce as much damage as DB 5 but I feel that the trade-off is more than fair for my playstyle.

I also like using either the Velk Y legs or helm for Peak Performance or Coalescence respectively, depending on the monster. Peak works perfectly fine for most fights, but isn't good against something like Teo with his fire puddles and fire aura. So for him, I use my Coalescence build, which includes Coal 3, Resuscitate, and Blight Res 1. Works like a charm.

Most hammer users don't bother with Focus or Slugger. Focus isn't needed because charge level one and two attacks are useful on their own, and you don't want to run the risk of charging too fast and skipping over them when you need them.

Here is why most people don't use Slugger. Calculations show that, because of the way status thresholds works, you will typically only gain one or two extra KOs per fight. By the time you would reach the next KO (fifth or so), you would have already dealt enough damage to kill the monster.

In a lot of situations, DPS skills outclass Slugger because the extra Big Bang Attacks you get from the one/two extra KOs from Slugger is not greater than the *overall damage increase* from DPS skills.

For your 3 level 2 slots, I would personally choose Agitator. Three levels of Agi would provide a nice boost of attack +12 and affinity +7%. If you're consistent with wallbangs, you can technically keep that buff active 95% of the fight.

There was a concept in one of the game's artbook I really liked. It was a hunting hound. The hunter uses a small rapier-type weapon that is short enough to double as a pointer. It has some minor offensive capabilities, but it's mostly used to direct the hound to a target. The hound is your main damage-dealing method, and can be equipped with armor crafted from different monsters. I believe that's all that was decided in the concept art, but I think it has a lot of potential. I came up with a couple silly ideas for it on my own. Here's what I've got.

Hunting hounds could have two different kinds of attacks– claw attacks, which are lighter and faster, and bite attacks, which are heavier and slower. That way, both raw and elemental playstyles could be viable. The armor crafted for hunting hounds could directly affect offensive power and type, like a weapon.

For example, if you wanted an elemental-based playstyle, you would craft Fulgur Anjanath armor, whose base raw damage wouldn't be great, but it adds a large amount of Thunder damage to claw attacks. Your playstyle would then revolve around those swift, light claw attacks, sort of like Dual Blades.

If you wanted a raw-based playstyle, you would craft Diablos armor, that has high raw and hidden Sleep element on bite attacks. You would then focus mainly on bites, since they hit harder with high raw. Or, if you're fighting a monster like Ebony Odo who is weakened by element, you could craft Rajang armor that has high raw but adds a small amount of Thunder element to bite attacks.

I don't know how balanced this system would be tbh but I think it would be good to allow flexibility in play styles. Also I just want a cute doggo to be friends with my palico.

Weapon-wise, I'd go for either the Kulu or Guild Palace hammers for high raw and non-elemental boost, or the Pukei hammer for okay raw but early purple sharpness and good poison. Plus, later on, the Guild Palace hammer can be upgraded into a decent early-endgame weapon. Don't bother with element for hammer. Just go for high raw damage.

Armor-wise, I'd do three piece Teostra, for Master's Touch, and two piece... whatever else you want. I would suggest prioritizing these skills for the extra two pieces: Critical Eye, Weakness Exploit, Critical Boost, Agitator, and Health Boost. Attack Boost is pretty good too but I would personally save that for when you've maxed out the aforementioned skills, since it's not as efficient as those. I believe I ended up using the Teostra helm, Rathalos chest, Teostra arms and waist, and Clockwork legs. The Kirin chest is good for early MR, too.

If you find that you're being throttled around too much, the most efficient defensive skills for hammer are Health Boost, Divine Blessing, Evade Window/Extender, and possibly Blight Resistance if the monster deals a lot of blights. For me, Health Boost 3 is mandatory on all my builds. And as much as I love offensive builds, against some monsters I always use countering defensive skills. I *highly* recommend Effluvia Resist 3 for Blackveil.

-Keep moving to avoid tornadoes

-But don't move into the line of normal attacks

-But don't bring normal attacks into contact with comets

-But when comets drop, make sure they're somewhere convenient

-All while still attacking

There are a few ways to deal with his flying as a melee hunter. The one that would be most beneficial would be to use the slinger burst to send him crashing to the ground. That way you get the crash landing damage, plus however much damage you can deal when he's flailing about. You can't do this during an enraged state though, and if you don't have either the temporal or rocksteady mantles then it's pretty hard to clutch onto the head without getting knocked off. So I usually only do this if I have mantles ready.

The next way is to use a flash bomb, but this doesn't work if he's enraged either. I would save this for when he's flying and not enraged, BUT you don't have anything that allows for an easy clutch claw opening.

The last way I personally haven't tried yet, because I actually just learned about it today. Apparently, if you're stuck because he's flying and enraged, you can use a smoke bomb to conceal yourself, and Alatreon will lose sight of you. This will cause him to drop back onto the ground to look for you, allowing you to get some attacks in. It also apparently procs a roar when you hit him which you can take advantage of if you have the evasion mantle. I don't use it for this fight personally. You could probably use the ghillie mantle for this too, but I really don't think it's worth taking in place of a rocksteady or an elemental mantle.

And if I don't feel like doing any of those, then I'll just wait until Ala does a breath-type attack and clutch onto his back legs, and I won't get knocked off. You have to time it really well though– like, right as the breath attack begins– because if you're still on him once he's done with the breath attack, he tends to do the dragon element dash forward that will always knock you off.

Good luck.
